name: Fencing
energy: Short explosive lunges and footwork bursts (about 2.5 s per point in sabre, 5 s in foil, 15 s in épée) on an aerobic base that has to last a long tournament day.
summary: Fencing is repeated lunging and fast changes of direction from an asymmetric stance, and most injuries are ankle sprains and lower-limb strains. The plan builds horizontal leg power and single-leg strength on both sides, strong hamstrings and adductors, and ankle control.

evidence.claim: In FIE competitions 72% of time-loss injuries were lower limb, ankle sprain was the most common single injury (25%), and épée had about half the injury risk of foil and sabre.
Standing broad jump was the strongest predictor of lunge velocity and change-of-direction speed in fencers, and single-leg jumps were 9% stronger on the front leg.
evidence.source: Turner et al. 2016, J Strength Cond Res

evidence.claim: Work:rest differs by weapon: about 1:1 to 2:1 in épée, 1:1 to 1:3 in foil and 1:5 to 1:6 in sabre.
evidence.source: Oates, Price & Bottoms 2023, J Elite Sport Perform

variants.name: Foil
variants.desc: Points last about 5 s with work:rest about 1:1 to 1:3; fast attacks and parries in a small target area.
variants.note: Your plan is the standard one, with footwork intervals of 5 s bursts and 10 s rest.

variants.name: Épée
variants.desc: Longest actions (about 15 s) and the most continuous footwork, with the lowest injury rate of the three weapons.
variants.note: Your gym plan stays the same; footwork intervals use longer 10-15 s efforts to match épée bouts.

variants.name: Sabre
variants.desc: Shortest, most explosive actions (about 2.5 s) with long rests, and a higher injury risk than épée.
variants.note: Your plan adds extra jumps and hamstring work, and footwork intervals use short 3 s bursts with long rests.

tests.name: Standing broad jump
tests.how: Two-foot take-off, stick the landing, measure to the back heel; best of 3.
tests.note: Best single predictor of lunge speed (Turner 2016). Bands are practice for men; women about 15-20% lower.

tests.name: Single-leg hop for distance
tests.how: Hop and stick on each leg, best of 3; compare front and rear leg.
tests.note: Elite fencers averaged 9% in favour of the front leg (Turner 2016). Over 15% is a flag (practice).

tests.name: Y-balance anterior reach
tests.how: Stand on one leg and reach forward with the other foot along a tape line; best of 3 each side.
tests.note: A difference over 4 cm is linked to lower-limb injury in other sports (Plisky 2006).

tests.name: Countermovement jump
tests.how: Hands on hips, jump mat or My Jump app, best of 3.
tests.note: Practice bands for men; women about 20% lower. Also a quick fatigue check on tournament weeks.

tests.name: Max lunge distance
tests.how: From en garde, lunge as far as you can and recover; measure front toe start to finish, best of 3.
tests.note: No verified norms; height dependent, so track your own change.

week: Tournament Saturday or Sunday: heavy lower strength Monday or Tuesday.
Lateral and upper session Wednesday at the latest.
Thursday and Friday: club fencing and a primer only.
No heavy lower work within 72 h of a tournament.
Day after a tournament: easy bike or walk and mobility.
primer: 2 x 3 broad jumps or lunges at full speed
Repeat a short footwork primer before the knockout rounds (direct elimination) after a long wait

lines: Last heavy lower lift 5-7 days before the event.
Gym volume down about 50%, keep the load.
Keep jumps, cut contacts by half.
Plan food, fluids and cooling between pool rounds and knockout bouts.

rules: Train both legs equally; the stance builds asymmetry.
Do the weaker leg first and match its reps on the other leg.
Nordic hamstring work all year, at least once a week in season.
No heavy lower work within 72 h of a tournament.
Previous ankle sprain: tape or brace for competition and keep balance work going.
Under 16: no depth jumps and no one-rep max (1RM) testing.
